chapter_theme: Holy ash (திருநீறு): wearing the ash Siva himself wears, as armour, drives off deeds and brings the Siva state; ash from the sacred fire changes the form and lineage of the pure who wear it. The chapter opens with a verse on the true sacred thread and tuft.
structure_note: The first verse (1665) is about thread and tuft, not ash, and nearly repeats 230; only 1666 and 1667 are on the ash.

1665.reading: Fools, you do not understand thread and tuft: the thread is Vedanta and the fine tuft is knowledge; Brahmins who keep to the one part will see the supreme soul, whether it is one or two, if they recite Om.
1665.nuance: The first two lines restate 230 plainly. பாலொன்றும் and ஓரொன்று இரண்டெனில் are obscure: perhaps 'whether the soul and the Supreme are one or two', a question Om is said to settle. Why the verse stands under holy ash is unclear.

1666.reading: If they wear with gladness, never letting it fade, the holy ash that is armour, which Kankala wears, deeds will not stay, the Siva state will come, and they will reach the beautiful holy feet.
1666.nuance: கங்காளன் is Siva bearing the skeleton, and கவசம் (armour) makes the ash a protection. மங்காமல் can mean wearing it without letting it fade, or without fail.

1667.reading: The ash from peepal, banyan and fig wood, its form changed in the spreading fire, makes the form of the pure, who have gained the feet of the partless and stainless one, into a high lineage like Brahma's.
1667.nuance: அரசுடன் ஆலத்தி is taken as peepal (அரசு), banyan (ஆல்) and fig (அத்தி), the woods of the sacrificial fire, and அக்காரம் as the ash; both readings are tradition's guess. The last line may mean the wearer gains Brahmin status, or that his form becomes like Brahma's.

links.note: Nearly the same verse: 230 asks whether thread and tuft are Brahman and says the real thread is Vedanta and the real tuft knowledge; 1665 repeats this and adds Om as the means of seeing the supreme soul.

1666 says those who gladly wear the holy ash that is armour (கவசத் திருநீற்றை) will find deeds do not stay (தங்கா வினைகளும்). Thiruppugazh 651 calls the poet a man of two deeds who never wore the true holy ash (மெய்த்திரு நீறிடா இருவினையேனை) and asks Murugan to smear it on him. Both join wearing the ash to release from deeds, one as promise, one as confession.

Kural 133 says conduct is noble lineage (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை) and its lapse becomes low birth. 1667 says the ash of the sacred woods makes the form of those who have gained the stainless one's feet a high lineage (உயர்குலம் ஆமே). Both say high குலம் is made rather than born; the Kural makes it by conduct, Tirumular by ash and grace.

source_issues: 1666: line 1 reads பூசுng, a garbled பூசுங்.
1665: a verse on thread and tuft, nearly repeating 230, stands at the head of the chapter on holy ash.
